[[File:Cochlearia officinal2.jpg|thumb|Illustration of ''Cochlearia officinalis'' in "Les Plantes potagères" Vilmorin 1925]]
'''''Cochlearia officinalis''''', '''common scurvygrass''', '''scurvy-grass''', or '''spoonwort''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Brassicaceae]]. The plant acquired its common name from the observation that it cured [[scurvy]].

==Description==
''Cochlearia officinalis'' is a [[biennial plant|biennial]]/[[perennial]],<ref name="wildireland"/> growing to {{convert|10|-|50|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}}.<ref name=Readers/> The stems are hairless and long stalked with fleshy leaves. The leaves are heart or kidney shaped, the lower stems leaves form a rosette around the base of the plant.<ref name=Readers/> Blooming from May to August,<ref name="pfaf">{{cite web |title=Cochlearia officinalis - L. |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Cochlearia+officinalis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171223102209/https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Cochlearia+officinalis |archive-date=2017-12-23 |access-date=24 December 2017 |publisher=Plants For A Future}}</ref> the flowers are small, white or lilac,<ref name="wildireland"/> with four daisy-like petals.<ref name=Readers/> The spherical seeds ripen from July to September.<ref name=pfaf/> The small, round seeds are reddish-brown.<ref name=Readers/> The flowers are [[hermaphrodite]] and the plant is [[self-fertile]].<ref name="pfaf" />

==Taxonomy==
It is commonly known as 'common scurvy-grass',<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=55 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=9780276002175}}</ref><ref name="rhs">{{cite web |title=''Cochlearia officinalis'' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/4056/i-Cochlearia-officinalis-i/Details|publisher=rhs.org.uk|access-date=24 December 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=David Chapman |title=Exploring the Cornish Coast |date=2008 |publisher=Alison Hodge |location=[[Penzance]] |isbn=9780906720561 |page=80}}</ref> 'scurvy-grass' and 'spoonwort'.<ref name="grin"/>

It was formally described by the Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753.<!-- p. 647 --><ref>{{cite web|title=Brassicaceae ''Cochlearia officinalis'' L.|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=281469-1|publisher=ipni.org|access-date=23 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="Plantlist">{{cite web|title=''Cochlearia officinalis'' L. is an accepted name|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2729901|date=23 March 2012|publisher=theplantlist.org|access-date=23 December 2017}}</ref>

The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''[[officinalis]]'' refers to the Linnaean term for plants with an established medicinal, culinary, or other use.<ref>{{cite book |author=Stearn, William T. |title=Botanical Latin |publisher=Timber Press (OR) |year=2004 |page=456 |isbn=0-88192-627-2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w0hZvTFJUioC&pg=PA456}}</ref>

It has one known subspecies, ''Cochlearia officinalis'' subsp. ''integrifolia'' <small>(Hartm.) Nordal & Stabbetorp</small>.<ref name="Plantlist"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Cochlearia officinalis Prague 2012 1.jpg|thumb|right|300px| Cochlearia officinalis in [[Prague]]]]
''Cochlearia officinalis'' is native to temperate Europe.<ref name="rhs"/><ref name="grin">{{cite web|title=Taxon: ''Cochlearia officinalis'' L. |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=11010|date=4 April 2012|publisher=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov|access-date=23 December 2017}}</ref>

===Range===
It is found within Eastern Europe, in the [[Russian Federation]], (within the [[Administrative centre#Russia|Administrative centre]] of [[Arkhangelsk]], [[Komi Republic|Komi]], [[Murmansk]] and [[Nenets Autonomous Okrug|Nenets]]). In Central Europe, within [[Belgium]], [[Germany]], [[Netherlands]] and [[Switzerland]]. In Northern Europe, within [[Iceland]], [[Denmark]], the [[Faroe Islands]], [[Finland]], [[Ireland]], [[Norway]], [[Sweden]] and the [[United Kingdom]], and in Southwestern Europe within [[France]].<ref name="grin"/>

It has also [[naturalised]] in other parts of Europe such as [[Italy]] and [[Spain]].<ref name="grin"/>

===Habitat===
It grows in the coastal and mountainous regions of Europe, including the Alps.<ref name="rhs"/> In Ireland, it prefers [[saltmarshes]], coastal cliffs and walls, and rocky, muddy seashores.<ref name="wildireland">{{cite web|title=Information on Common Scurvygrass|url=http://www.wildflowersofireland.net/plant_detail.php?id_flower=346&wildflower=Scurvygrass,%20Common |publisher=wildflowersofireland.net|access-date=24 December 2017}}</ref> In Northern Scandinavia, it grows in gravel beaches, crevices in beach cliffs and salt marshes.<ref name="Brandrud">{{cite journal|last1=Brandrud|first1=Marie K.|last2=Paun|first2=Ovidiu|last3=Lorenzo|first3=Maria T.|last4=Nordal|first4=Inger|last5=Brysting|first5=Anne K.|title=RADseq provides evidence for parallel ecotypic divergence in the autotetraploid Cochlearia officinalis in Northern Norway|journal=Scientific Reports |volume=7|issue=1|pages=5573|date=2017|doi=10.1038/s41598-017-05794-z|doi-access=free|pmid=28717144|pmc=5514025|bibcode=2017NatSR...7.5573B}}</ref>

==Ecology==
The flowers are pollinated by [[bees]], [[flies]], and [[beetles]]. The plant attracts wildlife and tolerates frost.<ref name="pfaf" />

==Uses==
It was once used by herbalists as a cure for [[scurvy]], as the plant contains [[Vitamin C]].<ref name="Readers" /> [[Nicholas Culpeper]] wrote of scurvygrass in his book ''Complete Herbal'' that its chief good effect is when used "by those that have the scurvy" and that it "is of singular good effect to cleanse the blood, liver and spleen, taking the juice in the Spring every morning fasting in a cup of drink".<ref name="wildireland" /> The plant was taken onboard ships in dried bundles or distilled extracts. Its very bitter taste was usually disguised with herbs and spices. Scurvygrass drinks and sandwiches were a popular in the UK until the mid-19th century, when [[citrus fruits]] became more readily available.{{Citation needed|date=January 2025}}

The leaves were made into a beer called scurvygrass ale,<ref name="Readers" /> which has been occasionally remade as a craft ale.<ref name="books">{{cite web|title=52 WEEKS OF HISTORICAL HOW-TO'S, WEEK 26: BREWING SCURVY GRASS ALE!|url=https://standrewsrarebooks.wordpress.com/2014/04/24/52-weeks-of-historical-how-tos-week-26-brewing-scurvy-grass-ale/|date=24 April 2014|access-date=24 December 2017}}</ref>
